name: Pubertal growth spurt timing

card.summary: The adolescent phase of fastest growth, when most of a person's final height is added, and the timing that decides when the height window is open and when it closes.
card.note: Timing varies widely between individuals; a late spurt is often a normal variant, and unusually delayed puberty is assessed by a paediatrician.

quick.overview:
The pubertal growth spurt is the period in adolescence when height increases fastest, driven by sex hormones and growth hormone/IGF-1. Most of the height a person will have as an adult is added in this window, so its timing matters for anyone who wants to be taller: it tells you whether growth is likely still to come or has finished.
Girls generally start the spurt earlier than boys, and boys' spurts start later, are slower to peak and last longer, which accounts for most of the average adult height gap between the sexes. Timing is strongly genetic, with nutrition the main environmental influence. Height-focused forums track signs such as shoe size, voice changes and yearly gains to guess where someone is in the spurt.
quick.how: In practice people estimate where they are in the spurt by tracking measured height over months, noting pubertal signs (body hair, voice change, genital development in boys; breast development and menarche in girls), comparing with parents' heights and growth charts, and sometimes asking a doctor for a bone-age X-ray of the hand and wrist. Looksmaxxing communities also discuss sleep, protein and calorie intake and sport as things that support growth during the window, and ask whether a second spurt might still arrive.
quick.risks: Rapid growth can bring growing pains, temporary clumsiness, and in some adolescents back problems such as adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, which tends to progress around the spurt. Delayed puberty is usually constitutional but can have medical causes, and clinicians evaluate it. Growth-hormone or other hormonal products used to chase extra height carry medical risks and are prescribed only for diagnosed conditions.

lead: The pubertal growth spurt is the stretch of adolescence in which a young person's height increases faster than at any time since infancy. It is the main period in which final adult height is built, so timing questions (when it starts, when it peaks, when it ends) are central to how people think about height, and to how they estimate how much growth is still to come [1][4].

Puberty generally begins around 10 to 11 years in girls and 11 to 12 in boys, and the spurt begins in the first half of it; in girls it comes after breast development and before the first period, while in boys it starts later, accelerates more slowly and continues longer before the growth plates fuse [1]. Males are on average about 2 cm shorter than females before puberty but about 13 cm taller as adults, a difference attributed mostly to the later and longer male spurt [1]. Estradiol drives the spurt and growth-plate closure in both sexes, and IGF-1 rising with growth hormone is thought to be a major mediator [1][24].

For people who want to look taller, the spurt is the window in which the most height is gained, which is why nutrition and overall health are the environmental factors researchers name as supporting growth during it, while the timing itself is mostly inherited [1][3]. Clinicians estimate where a young person stands in the spurt with growth charts, pubertal staging (the Tanner scale) and bone-age X-rays [16][20][21].

In looksmaxxing and height forums, the spurt is the subject of constant questions: whether it has begun, whether one is nearly finished, and whether another could still occur [11][12][13]. Sports scientists and paediatric endocrinologists study the same timing through measures such as age at peak height velocity and skeletal age [2][17].

Growth accelerates for roughly two to three years

angle.text: Adult height is largely decided in this window, so knowing where one is in the spurt tells people how much growth may remain. Sleep, nutrition and general health are discussed as supporting growth during it, while timing itself is mostly set by genetics.

paras: Growth in height proceeds fastest in infancy, slows through childhood and then accelerates again during puberty [3]. During the adolescent spurt, height velocity can reach about 8 to 12 cm per year, with peaks of around 9.5 cm per year in boys and 8.3 cm per year in girls reported in one overview [4]. Appetite often increases, and limbs may grow before the trunk, producing a temporary change in proportions [4].

The spurt is usually described by its onset, its peak height velocity (PHV), and the age at which growth stops. In girls the average age of maximal adult height is around 15, in boys around 18 [1]. Boys typically peak around 13 to 14 and girls around 11 to 12 [3].

Growth is usually described as three phases: rapid infant growth, steady childhood growth of several centimetres a year, and the adolescent acceleration, after which velocity falls to zero as the growth plates close [3][4]. Different body parts accelerate in sequence, with the feet and legs typically leading and the trunk following, which is why adolescents can look temporarily long-limbed [4]. The adolescent acceleration was first described in the nineteenth century and mapped precisely by mid-twentieth-century longitudinal studies [4][16][25].

sections.h: Origins of the concept and measurement
paras: Modern knowledge of the spurt rests on longitudinal studies that measured the same children repeatedly. British paediatrician James Tanner and colleagues produced growth standards and a five-stage rating of pubertal development: girls' data were quantified in 1969 and boys' data published in 1970 with W. A. Marshall, and the scheme is still the reference for pubertal staging by a trained examiner [20]. The 1976 longitudinal standards for height, height velocity and stages of puberty remain one of the most-cited growth datasets [16].

Skeletal maturity is the other main yardstick. Bone age compares an X-ray of the left hand and wrist with reference images; the Greulich and Pyle atlas first appeared in 1950 and was built on Brush Foundation Study children imaged between 1931 and 1942, while the Tanner-Whitehouse method (1962, revised 1975 and 2001) scores individual bones [21]. Combined with current height, bone age feeds tables such as Bayley-Pinneau that estimate adult height; the method has limits, including reference images from a restricted population, differences between assessors and a little radiation exposure [21].

Genetics account for at least 46% of variation in pubertal timing in well-nourished populations, with nutrition the strongest environmental influence [1]. Twin studies put the heritability of adult height itself at roughly 60 to 80% [3]. Severe malnutrition and neglect have the greatest effect during the critical growth periods [3]. Studies of stunted children in Bangladesh have examined how early-life stunting relates to later pubertal development [5].

Population averages also differ. One overview reports that children of Asian descent may reach skeletal maturity later than those of European descent, and that timing varies by ethnicity [4]. Because individuals vary widely, researchers and clinicians use several markers to estimate maturity, including skeletal age, secondary sex characteristics and anthropometric prediction of age at PHV [2].

Tempo differs even within a population. In the Kangwha cohort in South Korea, which followed 359 boys and 441 girls from 1986 to 1999, average-tempo boys peaked at about age 12 and girls at about 10, with early maturers about a year earlier and late-maturing boys about a year later [22]. Peak velocity was about 8.6 cm per year in average boys and 7.1 in average girls, and early-maturing children tended to show a higher peak, a difference statistically significant only in boys [22]. Final height did not differ between early, average and late groups in that study, and the authors called for further longitudinal work that also records pubertal stage [22]. A validation study of equations that predict age at peak height velocity reported limitations in early- and late-maturing boys and girls [2][17].

Rising estrogen, in males as well as females, promotes programmed death of growth-plate cartilage cells, so fewer cells are available for bone formation; growth slows and ceases once the plate is replaced by bone [24]. Complete fusion can occur as early as 12 in girls (most commonly 14 to 15) and as early as 14 in boys (most commonly 15 to 17) [24]. Population-level timing has also shifted over generations, and secular trends in age at menarche and height are a subject of growth research [1][3].

Delayed puberty is defined as no breast development by about 13.4 years in girls and no testicular enlargement by 14 years in boys; the most common cause is constitutional delay of growth and puberty, which is a variant of normal timing, while chronic illness or hormonal disorders account for others [6]. Clinicians assess history, growth records and pubertal staging, and boys may be offered treatment [6].

Randomised work on growth hormone therapy has looked at its effects on spontaneous sexual development in children treated for short stature [7]. Such treatment is a medical matter for diagnosed conditions.

Delayed puberty affects about 2% of adolescents and is more common in boys; constitutional delay, a healthy, inherited slower tempo in which bone age matches height, is the most common cause, followed by chronic illness or undernutrition, gonadal failure and hormone-pathway defects [23]. A hand X-ray for bone age, blood hormone tests and family history help separate these [23]. For constitutional delay, clinicians usually monitor and reassure; boys over about 14 with marked delay or distress may be offered short-term testosterone, and growth hormone and aromatase inhibitors are not recommended for this group [23]. Sources note that children with constitutional delay may end up a few centimetres shorter than their genetic target, though evidence is mixed, and that delay can cause distress, especially in boys [23].

Idiopathic short stature is the term for unexplained, markedly short height after standard evaluation; the manufacturer Eli Lilly proposed a threshold of 2.25 standard deviations below the mean when it sought FDA approval of growth hormone for the indication in 2003, and treatment has been debated on cost, expected gain and psychosocial benefit [25].

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis typically presents between about age 10 and the end of the growth spurt, and clinicians monitor curves during this period [8]. Idiopathic condylar resorption, a jaw-joint condition, predominantly affects young women around the pubertal spurt [9]. Orthodontists also use growth-spurt stage and cervical vertebral maturation to time treatments such as palatal expansion [10].

On looksmax.org, threads regularly ask whether a spurt has begun, how to tell if one is imminent and when the last spurt happened; titles include questions about a spurt not yet starting and about getting another one [11][12][13]. Typical posts give age, current height and parents' heights. One 14-year-old asks whether a spurt will still come given his height relative to his father's [11], and a 13-year-old describes fewer growth bursts than in earlier years and asks if that signals early puberty [26]. Replies commonly cite parents' heights, shoe size, voice changes and past yearly gains.

Another recurring thread type is the wish for 'one more' spurt near the end of the teens, where the replies mix encouragement, jokes and height estimates [27]. Some ask whether growth-hormone secretagogues such as MK-677 could produce a spurt [14]. Another thread describes a large late increase in height as a personal story [15].

Human research on growth-spurt timing includes longitudinal growth standards for height, height velocity and pubertal stages, a landmark 1976 dataset that is still widely cited [16]. Studies of youth athletes evaluate methods for estimating maturity status and age at PHV, and note that selection into sport follows a maturity-related gradient [2][17]. A randomised trial of calcium supplementation in adolescent girls examined iron status and age at menarche [18]. A registered study (NCT03363802) assesses the pubertal growth spurt in girls using finger bone and molar development [19].

A 1998 randomised trial of calcium supplementation in adolescent girls examined iron status and age at menarche [18]. In the Kangwha longitudinal cohort, final height was similar across early, average and late maturers [22]. Randomised work on growth hormone has looked at its effect on spontaneous sexual development in short-stature children [7]. Studies of stunted Bangladeshi children examined the link between early-life stunting and later pubertal development [5].

Practices that interact with the timing of the spurt include orthodontic treatments timed to growth-spurt stage [10]. Bone-age X-rays, parental mid-height calculators and growth charts are the standard tools for estimating remaining growth [16][21].

timeline.event: Kotelmann describes the adolescent acceleration of growth as a distinct phase, according to one overview [4].
First edition of the Greulich and Pyle hand-and-wrist bone-age atlas appears [21].
Tanner-Whitehouse skeletal maturity method first published; revised in 1975 and 2001 [21].
Tanner's staging of girls' pubertal development is quantified; boys' data follow in 1970 with Marshall [20].
Longitudinal standards for height, height velocity and stages of puberty are published in Archives of Disease in Childhood [16].
Kangwha cohort in South Korea follows 800 children through puberty [22].
A method for estimating maturity from anthropometric measurements (predicted maturity offset) is published [17].
Eli Lilly proposes a 2.25 standard deviation threshold for idiopathic short stature in its FDA growth-hormone submission [25].
A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine surveys assessment of biological maturation in youth athletes [2].

lore.intro: Forum users trade guesses about whether they are still growing and what might trigger another spurt [11][13].

claims.claim: A second or late growth spurt can still happen after a long plateau
claims.believers: Posters describe going months without growth and then gaining quickly, and ask how to recognise the signs of an imminent spurt [12][13].
claims.experts: Pubertal timing varies widely and constitutional delay is a recognised normal variant, with boys' growth continuing to about 18 on average [1][6].

claims.claim: MK-677 or similar compounds could trigger a growth spurt
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether MK-677 can help produce a spurt [14].
claims.experts: No trial tests this for appearance; growth-hormone treatment is studied only in children with diagnosed conditions [7].

claims.claim: Parents' heights and early signs predict how much spurt remains
claims.believers: Posters estimate their remaining growth from parental height, current height and pubertal signs [11].
claims.experts: Heritability of height is about 60-80%, and clinicians use bone age and height velocity to estimate maturity [3][2].

claims.claim: Sleep, protein and calories during the spurt let you reach your full genetic height
claims.believers: Height-focused posters say good sleep, enough food and sport while growing help them reach the top of their genetic range.
claims.experts: Genetics explain much of pubertal timing and adult height, with nutrition the main environmental influence and severe malnutrition having the largest effect in critical periods [1][3].

claims.claim: Early maturers end up taller than late maturers (or vice versa)
claims.believers: Forum members ask whether early signs of puberty, such as body hair before a big height gain, mean growth will end sooner [26].
claims.experts: The Kangwha cohort found final height did not differ between early, average and late maturers; boys with early timing showed a higher peak velocity [22].

claims.claim: Growth plates can be checked and growth is over when they fuse
claims.believers: Height-focused members commonly describe growth as finished once the growth plates have closed and ask how to tell whether theirs have.
claims.experts: Fusion occurs under estrogen, commonly at 14 to 15 in girls and 15 to 17 in boys, and bone age helps estimate remaining growth with stated limits [21][24].

claims.claim: Delayed puberty means a bigger final spurt
claims.believers: Late starters in threads hope the spurt is still to come and ask how much height it can add [11].
claims.experts: Constitutional delay is a normal variant, with final height near target in most cases and sometimes a few centimetres below it [23].
